summary: Silver sulfadiazine is a topical 1% cream used to prevent and treat wound sepsis in patients with second- and third-degree burns. It provides broad-spectrum antibacterial activity, including against Pseudomonas, by slow release of silver ions that act on the microbial cell membrane and DNA. Applied to cleaned, debrided burns once or twice daily under a thin layer, it is generally well tolerated, but significant systemic absorption can occur from large burn areas, raising the risk of sulfonamide toxicity (including blood dyscrasias, hepatic and renal effects, and kernicterus in neonates). It is contraindicated near term in pregnancy, in premature infants, and in neonates under 2 months.
indications: Prevention and treatment of wound sepsis in patients with second- and third-degree burns

dosage.d: Apply a layer about 1.6 mm (1/16 inch) thick to the cleansed, debrided burn
dosage.n: Use a sterile gloved hand; reapply to any area where cream is removed

dosage.d: Keep the burn covered with cream at all times; reapply as needed
dosage.n: Burn may be dressed or left exposed per protocol

dosage.d: Continue until satisfactory healing or until the site is ready for grafting
dosage.n: Bathing/whirlpool may aid debridement before reapplication

admin: Cleanse and debride the burn wound before each application
Apply with a sterile gloved hand to a thickness of approximately 1.6 mm (1/16 inch)
Keep the treated area covered with cream at all times; reapply if cream is rubbed or washed off
Continue treatment until the burn is healed or ready for grafting
For extensive burns, monitor for systemic sulfonamide effects (serum levels, CBC, renal/hepatic function)
moa: Silver sulfadiazine acts on the bacterial cell membrane and cell wall rather than purely through the antifolate mechanism of typical sulfonamides. On contact with wound fluid the compound slowly dissociates, releasing silver ions that bind to and disrupt microbial DNA and cell membranes, producing a bactericidal effect proportional to the amount of silver liberated. It has broad-spectrum activity against many gram-negative and gram-positive bacteria (including Pseudomonas aeruginosa) and is also active against yeast, helping to prevent and control burn wound infection.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to silver sulfadiazine, sulfonamides, or any component
Pregnant women approaching or at term
Newborn infants during the first 2 months of life (risk of kernicterus)
relative: Extensive burns where significant systemic absorption is expected
Renal or hepatic impairment (with large surface application)
Known sensitivity to other sulfonamide derivatives
monitor: Signs of systemic sulfonamide toxicity when used over large areas
Renal and hepatic function with extensive use
Serum sulfa concentrations in patients with extensive burns

preg: Sulfonamides cross the placenta and can cause kernicterus in the newborn. Silver sulfadiazine should not be used in pregnant women approaching or at term, or on extensive areas, unless the potential benefit clearly justifies the potential risk to the fetus.
lact: Sulfonamides are excreted in human milk and may cause kernicterus, particularly in jaundiced, ill, stressed, or premature infants and those with G6PD deficiency. Use with caution in nursing mothers; avoid where the infant is under 2 months of age or otherwise at risk.
renal: Systemically absorbed sulfadiazine is excreted by the kidneys; in patients with extensive burns or impaired renal function, sulfa and silver may accumulate. Monitor renal function and serum sulfa concentrations and watch for crystalluria when large areas are treated.
hepatic: When significant systemic absorption occurs (large burn surface), sulfonamide-associated hepatic effects, including hepatitis, may develop. Monitor liver function in patients treated over extensive areas and discontinue if hepatotoxicity is suspected.

major: Topical proteolytic enzyme (collagenase) debriding agents - silver may inactivate enzymatic debriders; avoid concurrent use
moderate: Oral hypoglycemics (sulfonylureas) - systemically absorbed sulfonamide may potentiate hypoglycemia
Phenytoin - systemic sulfonamide may increase phenytoin levels
minor: Cimetidine - reported to increase incidence of leukopenia with silver sulfadiazine
interactions.diagnostics: Can cause transient leukopenia (low neutrophils) within a few days of starting therapy; this usually recovers.

common: Local pain or burning on application
Skin discoloration (argyria-like greyish staining with prolonged use)
serious: Blood dyscrasias (hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia)

monitoring: Wound healing and signs of local or systemic infection
Complete blood count, especially white cell count, in early therapy
Renal and hepatic function when treating extensive burns
Serum sulfa concentrations if large surface areas are treated
Signs of sulfonamide hypersensitivity (rash, fever, mucosal lesions)
counsel: This cream is for skin/burn use only - do not swallow
It may sting briefly when applied; tell staff if pain is severe or persistent
Report any rash, fever, sore throat, mouth ulcers, or unusual bruising/bleeding
Prolonged use over large areas can occasionally tint the skin greyish
Avoid sun exposure of treated skin where possible (sulfonamide photosensitivity)
Keep the wound covered with cream as instructed and attend dressing changes
pk: Local antibacterial effect on contact with wound exudate
Systemic absorption variable; greater with large burn surface area
Absorbed sulfadiazine ~10 hours (prolonged in renal impairment)
Maintained while cream remains on the wound; reapply 1-2x daily
Store at controlled room temperature; avoid exposure to extreme heat
pearls: First-line topical agent for preventing burn wound sepsis; covers Pseudomonas
Contraindicated near term in pregnancy, in premature infants, and neonates <2 months - sulfonamide kernicterus risk
Transient leukopenia in the first few days is common and usually resolves without stopping; recheck CBC
Significant systemic sulfa absorption can occur from large burns - then full sulfonamide precautions apply
Do not use with enzymatic (collagenase) debriding agents - silver inactivates them
Avoid in G6PD deficiency due to hemolysis risk
missed: If a scheduled application is missed, clean the wound and apply the cream as soon as practical, then resume the usual schedule. Do not apply an excessively thick layer to compensate.
overdose: Topical overdose is unlikely, but extensive or prolonged application over large burn areas can lead to systemic sulfonamide toxicity (blood dyscrasias, hepatic and renal effects, crystalluria). Treat by discontinuing use, providing supportive care, ensuring adequate hydration to prevent crystalluria, and monitoring blood counts and organ function.
